title: Quinoa vs. Lentils: Protein, Fiber, and Carbs Compared

seo.title: Quinoa vs. Lentils: Protein, Fiber, and Carbs Compared
seo.meta_description: Per 100 g cooked, lentils provide about 9 g protein and 8 g fiber; quinoa about 4.4 g protein and 2.8 g fiber. Their carbohydrate totals are similar.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked quinoa and lentils for protein, fiber, carbohydrates, and calories.

excerpt: Lentils clearly lead on protein and fiber: per 100 g cooked they provide roughly 9 g protein and 8 g fiber, compared with about 4.4 g and 2.8 g in quinoa. Calories and carbohydrate are much closer, so the two foods play different roles on a plate.
content_html:
Quinoa and lentils often appear in the same plant-protein conversation, but they play very different roles on a plate. With surprisingly similar calories and carbohydrate per 100 g cooked, lentils provide about twice the protein and almost three times the fiber. Quinoa behaves more like a grain base and has an unusually balanced amino-acid profile for a pseudocereal.

Cooked nutrition per 100 g

QuinoaLentils
Calories~120~116
Protein~4.4 g~9 g
Carbohydrate~21 g~20 g
Fiber~2.8 g~8 g

Energy differs by only about 4 calories and carbohydrate by roughly 1 g. The difference that changes the meal is protein and fiber: lentils provide about 4.6 g more protein and more than 5 g extra fiber per 100 g.

At a 200 g serving, that becomes roughly 18 g protein and 16 g fiber from lentils versus about 9 g protein and 5–6 g fiber from quinoa.

Quinoa's advantage is different: protein quality

Quinoa contains all nine essential amino acids and is relatively rich in lysine compared with many cereal grains. That describes the pattern of its protein, not a large total amount.

Both statements can therefore be true: quinoa has an interesting amino-acid profile, and lentils still provide much more protein in a cooked serving.

Lentils can anchor the protein; quinoa is usually the base

A 180–200 g serving of lentils can make a substantial contribution to both protein and fiber. The same amount of quinoa provides less of each and often benefits from another protein source if the goal is a high-protein meal.

That does not make quinoa a poor choice. It simply puts it in a role closer to rice, bulgur, or other grains: energy, some protein, minerals, and texture.

You do not have to choose one or the other

Quinoa and lentils work especially well together. Quinoa gives the meal a separate, grain-like base while lentils add protein and fiber; vegetables, olive oil, nuts, or seeds can build the rest of the plate.

If the question is “which has more protein and fiber?”, lentils win clearly. If you want a versatile gluten-free grain substitute with a strong amino-acid profile, quinoa serves a different purpose. The comparison is useful precisely because they do not do the same job.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: Cooked lentils, about 9 g/100 g versus roughly 4.4 g/100 g for quinoa.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Lentils, close to 8 g/100 g versus about 2.8 g/100 g for quinoa.

faq.question: Which has more carbohydrate?
faq.answer: They are very similar by cooked weight, around 20–21 g per 100 g.
